nodes.name: Exporting engineer
nodes.description: Member of a delivery team who needs a bounded bulk extract of their own namespaces' logs — typically a couple of days across a set of pods, tens of gigabytes — as files they can download. Reads logs day to day in Grafana; comes to LogGate only for the bulk case.

nodes.name: Platform operator
nodes.description: Owns the quota configuration, the namespace-to-group mapping template and the audit trail. Reviews what was exported and by whom; approves exports above the size threshold where approval is required.

nodes.name: LogGate
nodes.description: The governed bulk log export system: authentication, per-namespace authorization, quota admission, asynchronous extraction and audited artifact delivery. Exists so that bulk extraction is neither a Grafana query nor a shared logcli credential.

nodes.name: LogGate UI
nodes.description: Vite + React single-page app built into the control plane's static resources, so it is same-origin with the API and holds a session cookie rather than a token. Users pick namespaces, pod and container globs and a time range, see a size estimate before committing, watch per-window progress, and collect the files. They never write LogQL. Built.

nodes.name: LogGate control plane
nodes.description: Spring Boot 4.1 / Java 25 service. Terminates the OIDC login as a backend-for-frontend, resolves which namespaces the caller may read, generates the LogQL selector server-side, sizes the request against Loki's volume API and plans it into windows, admits it against quotas, and serves artifact downloads, each one audited. Built. Beans are declared explicitly in configuration classes under config, with component scanning switched off. Serves /actuator (health and Prometheus metrics) on a separate management port, 9090, that the Service's http port, the Ingress and the Route never reach. Also serves the page's Activity report, read from PostgreSQL so it is exact across replicas.

nodes.name: LogGate extraction worker
nodes.description: Claims export windows from Postgres with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED under a heartbeat lease, pages Loki's query_range within the window, de-duplicates entries at the nanosecond boundary, and streams gzipped JSON lines straight into a multipart upload. Enforces cancellation and the byte cap mid-window rather than at the end. Runs on virtual threads inside the control-plane image under a separate role. Built.

nodes.name: LogGate PostgreSQL
nodes.description: System of record for jobs, windows, artifacts and the audit trail, and the work queue itself — windows are claimed with SKIP LOCKED rather than through a separate broker. Schema is applied by Liquibase at application startup. Built: the initial changeset creates export_job, export_window, export_artifact and audit_event.

nodes.name: Export artifact store
nodes.description: S3-compatible object storage (Versity S3 Gateway locally, in place of MinIO, which no longer publishes pullable images) holding the gzip parts and the manifest. Parts are written by multipart upload from a 5 MiB buffer, so a multi-gigabyte window never touches heap or disk. Downloads are served by presigned URL directly from storage; artifacts of cancelled and expired jobs are purged. Built. Compatible with MinIO, NetApp ONTAP S3 (9.11.1 or later, for presigned URLs) and StorageGRID: uploads use only payload signing modes those stores document, because the AWS SDK's default trailing checksums are switched off, and an internal certificate authority can be trusted for storage calls alone.

nodes.name: Keycloak
nodes.description: OIDC provider. Issues the identity and the group claims that the authorization model intersects with namespace labels. Integrated via the authorization code flow terminated server-side. The chart ships a local, dev-mode Keycloak with seeded teams and users for development; production points at an existing instance. In open access mode it also grants the one client role that opens every log: LogGate reads the caller's effective client roles from resource_access.<client>.roles in the access token at sign-in, so a role granted to a group reaches every member with no mapper changes.

nodes.name: Kubernetes API
nodes.description: Authoritative source of the namespace-to-team mapping in team-label access mode. LogGate watches namespaces through an informer and reads the team label (for example xyz.com/team: platform), rendering the owning group name from a configurable template such as ad-{team}-{env}. Authorization fails closed when the informer has not synced. Only this cluster's API: when Loki holds several clusters' logs, team-label mode pins every export to this cluster, because ownership elsewhere is not visible from here. Not used at all in open access mode, which creates no client and no RBAC. Built.

nodes.name: Grafana Loki
nodes.description: The log store and its read path. LogGate uses two of its APIs: index/volume_range to size an export before running it, and query_range to fetch it. Exports are pinned to their own tenant or read pool so that a large extraction cannot starve interactive Grafana queries. Deployed in the local stack as a single binary with volume_enabled. It may hold several clusters' logs, told apart by a configurable stream label (commonly cluster); in open access mode its label values API is also how LogGate discovers which clusters and namespaces exist.

nodes.name: Grafana Alloy
nodes.description: Log collection agent. Discovers pods through the Kubernetes API and tails their logs via the API rather than host mounts, labelling each stream with namespace, pod and container — the labels the whole authorization and selector model depends on. Deployed in the local stack as a DaemonSet.

nodes.name: Grafana
nodes.description: Where teams read logs normally. Modelled because it defines LogGate's boundary: anything a team can answer with a dashboard query should not become an export job. LogGate ships a dashboard for its own metrics (deploy/helm/loggate/dashboards/loggate.json), loaded by Grafana's sidecar from a ConfigMap when metrics.dashboard.enabled is set; the local stack does so.

nodes.name: Prometheus-compatible metrics store
nodes.description: Any store with the Prometheus HTTP API: Prometheus, Thanos, Mimir or OpenShift's thanos-querier. Two roles. It scrapes LogGate's metrics from the management port for the Grafana dashboard. And it is where LogGate lists pods from: a series with one entry per pod (kube-state-metrics' kube_pod_info by default; the selector and its pod, namespace and cluster labels are configuration) read through the series API, for the chosen namespaces over the export's own range. Optional: without pods.metricsUrl the pod pattern is the only way to narrow by pod. Deployed in the local stack as Prometheus with kube-state-metrics, labelling kube-state-metrics' series with the cluster name. Built.

nodes.name: Kubernetes cluster
nodes.description: The deployment target. Locally a k3d cluster created by deploy/local/deploy.sh with ingress-nginx; in production any conformant cluster or OpenShift, where openshift.enabled leaves out fixed IDs for the restricted-v2 SCC and route.enabled serves the application through a Route. In open access mode LogGate need not run in any of the clusters whose logs it serves.

nodes.name: Other clusters shipping to Loki
nodes.description: Clusters whose log shippers send to the same Loki, each stamping its streams with the cluster label. LogGate has no credentials for, and needs no network path to, any of them: in open access mode their namespaces are discovered from Loki's index, and in team-label mode they are excluded by pinning every export to LogGate's own cluster. Simulated locally by deploy/local/seed-remote-cluster.sh.

relationships.description: Submits an export as a structured request — namespaces, pod and container selectors, time range, optional line filter — watches per-window progress, and collects the artifacts when the job is ready.
The normal path. Interactive log reading stays in Grafana; LogGate deliberately does not compete with it.
Reviews the audit trail, inspects and cancels running jobs, and approves exports that exceed the size threshold requiring a second person.
Same-origin JSON API calls carrying the session cookie. The SPA is served by the control plane itself, so there is no CORS surface and no access token in browser storage.

OIDC authorization code flow terminated server-side. In team-label mode the group claims are one half of the authorization decision and namespace labels the other; in open mode the client role in the access token is the whole of it.

Team-label access mode only. Watches namespaces and caches the team label per namespace. A namespace with no label, or one whose rendered group is absent from the caller's claims, is refused; the cache never fails open when the watch is stale.
Writes the job and its windows in one transaction at submit time, reads progress, and appends audit events. Hand-written SQL through JdbcClient; no ORM.
Calls index/volume_range with the generated selector to size the export before anything runs. That estimate is what makes the quota decision honest and what sets the window duration.

Claims windows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, heartbeats a lease while genuinely progressing, and records bytes and entries per window. A worker that dies has its windows reclaimed when the lease lapses.

Pages query_range forward within one window, carrying forward the identities of entries sharing the last nanosecond so the inclusive start bound does not duplicate them. Concurrency is bounded per job and globally, and backs off on 429 so a large export degrades itself rather than starving interactive queries.
Streams each window's entries through gzip into a multipart upload at a deterministic key, so a retried window overwrites its part rather than appending to it. Nothing is buffered to disk or heap.
Assembles per-stream files from window parts with UploadPartCopy, writes the manifest, mints short-lived presigned URLs, streams the proxied ZIP64 variant, and sweeps expired artifacts.

Bulk downloads go directly to object storage over presigned URLs, so tens of gigabytes never traverse the control plane. Authorization is re-checked when the URLs are minted, not only when the job was submitted.
Discovers pods and tails container logs through the API, which is what lets the same collection config work unchanged on k3d and on a managed cluster.

Pushes log streams labelled with namespace, pod and container. Those three labels are the vocabulary of every LogGate selector and every authorization decision. Each cluster's shipper also sets the cluster label.
Interactive queries. Shares the store with LogGate but not the read pool, which is the point of pinning exports to their own tenant.
What LogGate itself owns and ships. Keycloak, Loki, Alloy and Grafana are dependencies it integrates with, not parts of it.

Everything runs in-cluster locally. In production the control plane must stay in-cluster because the namespace watch is a Kubernetes API client; Postgres, object storage and Keycloak are commonly external.
Push log streams labelled with cluster, namespace, pod and container. The cluster label is the only thing that tells two clusters' same-named namespaces apart.

Open access mode only: asks the label values API which clusters, and which namespaces within them, have logged recently. Answered from the index, cached briefly, and served stale rather than failing when Loki blips. It lists what may be chosen; the client role, not this list, is what grants access. Namespaces are asked for only once clusters are chosen, never across every cluster on page load.

Lists the pods that ran in the chosen namespaces, and clusters, over the export's range: GET /api/v1/series with the configured selector plus namespace and cluster matchers escaped as regex literals. Authorized as an export of those namespaces would be, cached for a minute, served stale on failure. Optionally with a tenant header, a service-account bearer token and a CA of its own.

Scrapes /actuator/prometheus on the management port, found by prometheus.io annotations or a ServiceMonitor. No session is needed because the port is never published; the NetworkPolicy admits scrapers to it alone.
The LogGate dashboard's queries: queue depth, submissions and refusals, outcomes by failure code, throughput, window and Loki page latency, throttling and JVM health.

The drift was entirely in what is built versus designed, plus two deployment facts worth recording: the OIDC issuer URL must be byte-identical for browser and application, and beans are wired explicitly rather than scanned.
generated-from.reconciled-2026-09-20-m3: Structure unchanged again: the control-plane-to-loki-volume and worker-to-loki-query relationships already described what M3 implemented. Two constraints were discovered by building it and are recorded in extraction-model and known-limitations.

Removed the single-api-replica limitation, resolved when sessions moved to PostgreSQL as JSON. Recorded object storage compatibility and OpenShift support on the existing nodes.

implementation-status.built: M1 foundation: bootstrap, Liquibase schema, actuator health, a JaCoCo gate at 95% LINE and BRANCH proven to fail on uncovered code, a Helm chart with extraObjects, a Jib image build with no Dockerfile, and deploy/local/deploy.sh standing up k3d with Loki, Alloy, Grafana and an S3 server (MinIO then, Versity S3 Gateway now). M2 authentication and authorization: Keycloak OIDC as a backend-for-frontend, the namespace informer and group-template resolution, the fail-closed authorizer and the audit trail. M3 extraction engine: the Loki client with bounded retry and Retry-After handling, the glob-based selector builder, the volume-driven window planner, the paging de-duplicator, and POST /api/exports/estimate wiring them together behind authorization. M4 execution: the Postgres work queue with SKIP LOCKED claims and heartbeat leases, workers streaming gzip parts to object storage, mid-window cancellation and byte caps, layered admission quotas, job progress and cancellation endpoints, and the finalizer that publishes finished jobs and purges cancelled ones. M5 delivery and UI: the manifest with per-part counts and checksums, presigned download URLs, a generated verify-as-you-go download script, a streamed ZIP that stores rather than re-deflates the parts, the retention sweeper, and the React SPA. M6 hardening: shared sessions removing the single-replica limit, export metrics and queue gauges, NetworkPolicy templates, sampled line-filter estimates, the reworked UI, and the per-team rolling daily budget. Since M6: CA certificates from a Secret or a ConfigMap; namespaces listed only after clusters are chosen in open mode; pod listing from a Prometheus-compatible metrics store with a configurable series; a management port for metrics; a Grafana dashboard shipped with the chart; the in-app Activity page; and a redesigned export form whose pickers scale to tens of clusters. Then: download auditing with an administrators' audit page, an administrator client role gating it and the Activity page, a switch for pod patterns, and a Mimir compatibility check. Then: a per-export choice of JSON or raw output, OIDC RP-initiated sign-out, exports that can no longer be downloaded marked as such, pods matched by a label filter after the stream selector, and searchable dropdowns for long lists. Then: sign-out returning to the landing page, and the byte cap and team budget counted in log bytes, the estimate's units, rather than the larger JSON written. Then the query-bar layout: a side rail, the export as one line of chips each with its own panel, the size asked for as the choices settle, and exports as a searchable table with Run again.
implementation-status.designed-not-built: Server-side assembly of the parts into one file per stream with UploadPartCopy, which is an optimisation rather than a missing capability.
implementation-status.milestones: M1 foundation, M2 auth and namespace authorization, M3 extraction engine, M4 queue, quotas and lifecycle, M5 delivery and UI (all done) / M6 hardening and a verified multi-gigabyte export.

extraction-model.unit-of-work: A time window. The job's range is split into fixed windows sized from the volume estimate so each lands in the hundreds of megabytes. Window i of job J always covers exactly [t_i, t_i+1) and always writes the same object keys.
extraction-model.why-idempotent-windows: Determinism per window buys crash recovery, at-least-once workers with exactly-once artifacts, accurate progress as windows_done/windows_total, and parallelism with no coordination between workers — from one property rather than four mechanisms.
extraction-model.boundary-dedup: Loki's start bound is inclusive and several entries can share a nanosecond, so paging forward by last-timestamp duplicates the entries at that instant. The pager carries forward the identities of entries at the page's maximum timestamp and skips them next page. This is the highest-risk code in the system and carries the heaviest test weight.
extraction-model.back-pressure: Bounded concurrency per job and globally, reduced additively on sustained 429s. A large export slows itself instead of starving Grafana.
extraction-model.quota-abort: Bytes are counted as they are written, so a job exceeding its cap is killed mid-flight rather than discovered afterwards. This is the capability that decided the architecture (see rejected-options).
extraction-model.page-limit-constraint: The query page limit must exceed the number of entries that can share one nanosecond. Loki's API has no offset, so a query starting at that nanosecond returns the same first `limit` entries every time and paging cannot advance. The pager detects that it has stopped advancing and fails loudly rather than silently truncating the export.
extraction-model.selector-generation: Pod and container filters are globs: every character except * and ? is escaped into a literal. That removes LogQL injection and regex denial-of-service as categories rather than defending against them case by case. Sizing uses the stream selector without the line filter, because a filter reduces what is written but not what Loki reads, and the quota should be set against what is read. Pods picked from the list become an alternation of regex literals; a value that is not a valid pod name is refused rather than escaped, and picking pods and giving a pattern together is refused. The pod is matched by a label filter after the stream selector rather than a matcher inside it, so it matches whether the pod is an indexed label or structured metadata; the index then sizes the namespace and the pod filter's selectivity is sampled.

authorization-model.rule: A namespace labelled xyz.com/team: <team> is readable by the group rendered from a configurable template, for example ad-{team}-{env} giving ad-platform-dev.
authorization-model.source-of-truth: The Kubernetes API, watched and cached, not the token and not a static config. Group membership comes from Keycloak; the namespace-to-group mapping does not.
authorization-model.fail-closed: An unlabelled namespace, an unresolvable template or a stale cache refuses the request. There is no configuration in which an unknown namespace is readable.
authorization-model.no-logql-from-users: The API accepts a structured request and generates the selector itself, which removes the LogQL injection class entirely rather than defending against it. Free-form LogQL was considered and rejected for this system; a query-enforcing proxy such as loki-label-proxy would be required to reintroduce it safely.
authorization-model.download-time-recheck: Entitlement is re-evaluated when presigned URLs are minted. A 48-hour artifact must not outlive the access that produced it.
authorization-model.group-claim-normalisation: Keycloak emits group claims as full paths (/ad-platform-dev) unless the mapper is reconfigured, and directory-derived names vary in case. Group comparison strips the path and ignores case, so an entitlement is never lost to a leading slash.
authorization-model.issuer-url-identity: The issuer URL the browser is redirected to and the one the application resolves must be identical, because Keycloak puts the former in the id_token's iss and Spring validates the callback against the registered redirect_uri. Locally that means the ingress listens on the same port the browser uses and the application resolves that hostname to the ingress.
authorization-model.access-modes: Two, chosen by access.mode. team-label: teams export the namespaces labelled as theirs, read from this cluster's Kubernetes API, pinned to this cluster when Loki holds several. open: every namespace Loki holds, from every cluster, to holders of one client role on LogGate's OIDC client, typically granted through a Keycloak group; namespaces become optional, none meaning all; budgets are charged to the person because there are no teams. Open mode refuses to start without a role, so it can never mean every log to every signed-in user.
authorization-model.administrators: Holders of access.adminRole (default loggate-admin), a client role on LogGate's OIDC client read like the open-mode role but independent of it, see the Activity report and the download audit trail across everyone's exports, in either mode. A blank role makes nobody an administrator.

quota-model.submit-time: Maximum time range, maximum namespaces and streams, and estimated bytes from index/volume_range.
quota-model.runtime: A hard byte cap checked every few thousand entries rather than at the end of a window, so an over-limit export stops early instead of being written in full and then rejected. The cap carries headroom over the estimate because the range keeps receiving logs while the export runs, and it is recorded on the job so a job is judged against the limit it was admitted under.
quota-model.concurrency: Per user, per team and global concurrent job limits, plus a cap on simultaneous Loki queries originating from LogGate.
quota-model.budget: A rolling per-team budget, not a calendar one: no midnight cliff and no question about whose midnight. It counts bytes written plus the estimate of admitted-but-unfinished exports, because counting only finished ones would let ten large jobs start at once and stay under budget by virtue of none having finished. Failed exports are excluded - a team should not lose budget to something that produced nothing usable. An export spanning several teams is charged in full to each: a team that took part in pulling the data caused all of it, and splitting the cost would let one export slip under every budget it touches.
quota-model.storage: Artifact TTL of 24-48 hours swept by the control plane, with an object-store lifecycle rule as backstop so a broken sweeper cannot leak log data indefinitely.
quota-model.team-attribution: Teams are resolved from the namespace labels when a job is admitted and stored on the job rather than re-derived later. The budget is an accounting question about the past, and re-deriving would let a relabelled namespace quietly rewrite who spent what.

rejected-options.synchronous-streaming: Stream a ZIP to the browser with no object store and no workers. Rejected: a single connection for hours, no resume, a retry restarts tens of gigabytes, and quotas can only be advisory.
rejected-options.logcli-kubernetes-job: One logcli Job per export. Rejected as the primary engine: it needs tens of gigabytes of staging disk because --merge-parts reads its own part files back, gives only file-count or stderr progress, cannot enforce a precise byte cap, and spreads Loki and object-store credentials into per-export pods. Its correctness advantage is real and it remains the fallback engine.
rejected-options.logcli-per-window: Keep the window planner but invoke logcli once per window, so Grafana owns the pagination. Genuinely attractive and was the standing recommendation; not chosen — the decision was to own a pure-Java data path with no subprocess in it.
rejected-options.direct-object-store-read: Bypass the read path and read chunks from Loki's storage directly. Not rejected, deferred: it couples to the storage schema and misses logs still in ingesters, but it is the intended second tier for the very largest exports.
rejected-options.chosen: Asynchronous job service with an extraction engine written in Java, kept behind an interface so the logcli and direct-storage engines can be substituted per size tier without touching authorization, quotas or the UI.
rejected-options.per-cluster-kubernetes-api: For open access across clusters, reading each cluster's Kubernetes API for labels. Rejected: it needs credentials for and a path to every cluster, which running beside a central Loki avoids; Loki already knows every cluster and namespace.
rejected-options.open-mode-group-gate: Gating open mode on a group. The client role was chosen: it is scoped to LogGate's client, and a group can still grant it to every member.

governance.coverage: JaCoCo gates LINE and BRANCH at 0.95, wired into `gradle check`. The gate was verified to fail on deliberately uncovered code rather than assumed to work.
governance.supply-chain: Images are built by Jib from compiled classes — no Dockerfile and no container runtime in the build — with a fixed creation time so an unchanged tree produces a byte-identical image.
governance.audit: audit_event is a first-class table rather than application logs, because who exported production logs is a record that must outlive log retention. Downloads are audited by how the data left: the streamed .zip as a download, and the script and per-file presigned links as the issuing of links, since those files are fetched from object storage directly. Rows carry the export's namespaces, clusters and size so they outlive the job.

modelling-notes.granularity: One node per deployable process, plus the actors and the external systems LogGate integrates with. The namespace resolver, quota engine, window planner and LogQL builder are components inside loggate-api and are described rather than modelled as nodes.
modelling-notes.worker-packaging: loggate-worker is a separate node because it is a separately scaled Deployment, even though it ships in the same image as the control plane under a different role.
modelling-notes.object-store-node-type: export-object-store is typed database for want of an object-storage type in the CALM node-type enum; it is S3-compatible object storage, not a relational store.
modelling-notes.interfaces: Per-node host/port interfaces are omitted while ports are environment-configured, following the METAL-X model. Add host-port-interfaces when concrete deployment config is modelled.
modelling-notes.excluded: Loki's internal topology (gateway, querier, ingester, index and chunk stores) is folded into the loki node: LogGate integrates with its read API, and modelling its internals would document Grafana's architecture rather than this one.
modelling-notes.companion-doc: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md is the prose front door and explains the why; this CALM model is the structural source of truth.

bean-wiring.rule: No stereotype annotations. Every bean is declared with @Bean in a configuration class under com.opentooling.loggate.config, and the application class uses @SpringBootConfiguration with @Import rather than @SpringBootApplication, so nothing is component-scanned.
bean-wiring.why: The object graph is readable in one place instead of being inferred from annotations spread across packages.
bean-wiring.exception: Controllers keep @RestController because request mapping is derived from it, but they are registered as beans in WebConfig like everything else.

known-limitations.lokistack-gateway: The OpenShift Logging LokiStack gateway requires OpenShift bearer tokens, which the Loki client does not send; point LogGate at Grafana's Loki gateway or query frontend.

execution-model.queue: Windows are claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so many workers take work concurrently without coordinating, each skipping rows another holds rather than waiting behind them.
execution-model.leases: A claim carries a lease renewed by heartbeat while the window genuinely progresses. Nothing detects a dead worker; its lease simply stops being renewed and the window becomes claimable again.
execution-model.idempotency: A part's object key is derived from the job and window index alone, never from an attempt or a timestamp, so a window run twice overwrites its part instead of duplicating it. Completing a window twice is counted once.
execution-model.byte-accounting: Counted in log bytes, the lines as Loki measures them and so the estimate's units, rather than the JSON written around them, which runs two to three times larger; the cap and the team budget both use this count, and bytes written is kept only for reporting. The running total is the job's tally when the window was claimed plus what the window has produced. Under concurrency that under-counts what other windows are writing, so the cap is approached rather than enforced to the byte - the alternative being a shared counter updated per entry.
execution-model.cancellation: A flag on the job, noticed between pages. The finalizer closes a cancelled job only once no worker still holds a window, then purges its parts: a cancelled export is not a partial export.

delivery-model.two-paths: Presigned URLs keep tens of gigabytes out of the control plane entirely, which is the only sensible way to move an export that size. A proxied ZIP is the convenience path and is deliberately second best, because every byte passes through the application.
delivery-model.download-script: Tens of gigabytes is not a browser activity, so the generated script resumes, retries and checks SHA-256 rather than presenting a page of links to click one at a time.
delivery-model.archive-encoding: ZIP entries are STOREd rather than deflated, because the parts are already gzipped. That requires each entry's size and CRC before its data, which is why the CRC is recorded when the part is written rather than recomputed at download time.
delivery-model.manifest: Written before a job is advertised as ready: the selector, exact range, per-part counts and checksums, and any caveats. An export nobody can verify is not finished, so a job whose manifest cannot be written stays unpublished.
delivery-model.caveats: The manifest states what it cannot guarantee - for instance that a range reaching within fifteen minutes of the present may be missing entries still held in Loki's ingesters. Saying so is worth more than implying a completeness the export cannot have.
